title: Learning to Prepare Molecular Ground States with Transformer Models
authors: Alex Koziell-Pipe, Jasmine Brewer, Jem Guhit, Marwa H. Farag, Kripa Panchagnula, Gabriel Laude, Fabian Finger, Carlo Gaggioli, Ludmila Szulakowska, Oliver J. Backhouse, Christos Papalitsas, Jason G. Mustakis, Thomas Soini, David Munoz Ramo, Stephen Clark, Elica Kyoseva, Enrico Rinaldi
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a key component of many quantum algorithms. Performing this step efficiently is essential for realizing practical quantum advantage in quantum chemistry applications. Iterative algorithms like ADAPT-VQE can produce shallow ground-state preparation circuits, but become computationally prohibitive for the larger molecules relevant to materials science and pharmaceutical development. Here, we introduce ADAPT-GQE, a generative AI framework that learns to synthesize ground-state preparation circuits for electronic structure calculations. We first use ADAPT-VQE to generate high-quality reference circuits, which are then used as targets for training models for circuit generation. Once trained, the model can efficiently propose and score circuits, enabling reinforcement learning (RL) to drive circuit generation accuracy beyond the accuracy of the ADAPT-VQE training data. This pipeline achieves order-of-magnitude reductions in circuit generation time relative to ADAPT-VQE while maintaining comparable or improved state-preparation accuracy. We demonstrate ADAPT-GQE on imipramine, a well-established tricyclic antidepressant that serves as a representative, challenging target for computational modelling in drug stability protocols. We execute generated circuits on Quantinuum Helios-1, representing a milestone for AI-generated quantum chemistry circuits on state-of-the-art quantum hardware. These results establish a pathway toward automated quantum circuit synthesis for utility-scale quantum computational chemistry.
summary: The paper introduces ADAPT-GQE, an AI framework that uses Transformer models to automatically synthesize efficient quantum circuits required for calculating molecular ground states. By training on existing high-quality data and using reinforcement learning, it drastically reduces the time needed compared to state-of-the-art iterative methods like ADAPT-VQE. This establishes a pathway toward automated, scalable quantum chemistry simulations on modern hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is developing scalable methods for quantum state preparation, specifically calculating molecular ground states, because existing iterative algorithms are computationally prohibitive for large molecules.
main_result: The proposed ADAPT-GQE framework achieves order-of-magnitude reductions in circuit generation time compared to ADAPT-VQE while maintaining or improving state-preparation accuracy on challenging molecules like imipramine.
method: The authors use a generative AI approach, training Transformer models (like Gemma) on reference circuits generated by ADAPT-VQE. Reinforcement Learning is then employed to refine circuit generation beyond the initial training data's scope.
model_or_system: The physical system is molecular quantum chemistry, using Hamiltonians derived from molecules like imipramine. The methodology involves mapping these Hamiltonians into a format suitable for large language models (LLMs) to predict optimal quantum circuits.
key_observables: Energy accuracy ($	ext{E}_{	ext{pred}}$ vs $	ext{E}_{	ext{ref}}$ in mHa), circuit generation time, and the number of required quantum gates/operators.
important_parameters: Qubit count (up to 16 qubits), target energy tolerance ($\epsilon$), and hardware platform (Quantinuum Helios-1).
main_assumptions: The primary reward function relies on computationally expensive reference energies (CASCI or CCSD) for training, though an alternative reward function was shown to be effective.
figures_summary: Figures detail the conformational sampling of imipramine using MD/NEB; tables compare computational costs and energy accuracies between ADAPT-VQE and the Transformer models across various qubit counts.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the limitations of VQE/ADAPT-VQE, details the data generation pipeline (MD/NEB for diverse conformers), presents the LLM architecture for Hamiltonian encoding, and finally demonstrates performance gains via training and RL fine-tuning on hardware.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the resource bottleneck in applying quantum computation to chemistry by replacing iterative optimization with a learned generative model, which is highly relevant for scaling quantum algorithms beyond small test cases.

Fig. 2: Operator counts for each dataset. Number of operators from the operator pool for the 12- (a), 14- (b), and 16-qubit (c) systems in the ADAPT-VQE training data. The 12- and 14-qubit cases use a UCCGSD pool with energy thresholds defined as the difference from CASCI, while the 16-qubit case uses a UCCSD pool with error measured relative to CCSD.

Fig. 3: Trained-from-scratch transformer architecture and training. (a) ADAPT-VQE ground-state operator sequences are tokenized, with operators and numerical digits represented as individual tokens. Pauli-term coefficients from the molecular Hamiltonian are encoded with a residual MLP and interleaved within the token sequence before processing by the Gemma 3 transformer. (b) During pre- training, the model is trained for next-token prediction on ADAPT-VQE-generated sequences. During post-training, the model is iteratively refined through RL and super- vised fine-tuning on model-generated sequences.

Fig. 4: Pretrained NVIDIA Nemotron architecture and training. (a) ADAPT-VQE ground-state operator sequences are represented by their corresponding operator-pool indices and coefficients, and tokenized using the standard BPE tok- enizer. The coefficients of the Pauli terms in the molecular Hamiltonian are encoded with a residual MLP and prepended to the token sequence before being processed by the Nemotron Nano transformer. (b) The pretrained model is first adapted to the operator language through continual pretraining and then specialized for circuit gen- eration via supervised fine-tuning on ADAPT-VQE-generated sequences.
